lesson.title: LLMs for data systems: semantic operators with measurable quality
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Treat each model call as a costly, fallible operator with an explicit input, output and evaluation target.
goals: Distinguish LLM-assisted database control from LLM-powered data processing.
Calculate filter/cascade costs without assuming quality is unchanged.
Evaluate semantic pipelines against human labels and reference algorithms separately.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
You have 20,000 support notes and want the 2025 notes about battery overheating. Reading every note with a large model sounds straightforward, but how would you know it found the right notes, and which work can safely be skipped? We will answer those questions before discussing a system name.

Recall filtering and operator order from lessons 2–3 and 15. Paper calculations require no model or paid service. All traces and prices below are hypothetical teaching examples. This is supplemental practice, not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment; assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Two directions, two correctness problems
sections.html:
Start with a familiar SQL request: find overheating notes from 2025. An LLM might draft SQL for us. The DBMS can check syntax and execute it correctly, but an incorrect join may duplicate notes or a wrong date boundary may exclude December. Valid execution does not prove that the question was interpreted correctly. This is an LLM assisting DBMS control.

Now keep SQL's date filter but ask a model whether each note describes overheating. The model is acting on data as an operator. We must define positive, negative and uncertain labels, require evidence spans, and decide how errors are checked. Extraction, semantic joins, ranking and aggregation have similar issues: a natural-language instruction is not yet an unambiguous correctness rule.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) first retrieves context and then generates an answer. Retrieval can miss evidence and generation can contradict it; this does not supply transactional database guarantees. Record snapshot, model/embedding versions, prompts and retrieval settings. Document text remains input data, including any text pretending to give tool instructions. Keep question interpretation, SQL execution, semantic labels and grounded answers as separate checks.

Key takeaway

SQL execution correctness, interpretation of the question, semantic-label quality and grounded answer quality are separate checks.

sections.title: Worked example: push a cheap filter before an expensive operator
sections.html:
Work through the 20,000-note collection. A trustworthy date field retains 4,000 notes from 2025. Classifying every note at an assumed $0.002 costs 20,000×0.002=$40. Date filtering first costs 4,000×0.002=$8. We saved calls because excluded dates cannot answer this specific question. If the date field is wrong or excluded notes supply necessary context, that rewrite needs reconsideration.

Next let a cheap model classify all 4,000 at $0.0002 each: $0.80. Route 25%, or 1,000 uncertain notes, to the expensive model: $2.00. Total=$2.80 before calibration, labeling, retries and optimization. A confident false negative is not routed, so the saving can hide missed overheating notes.

Count against independent labels. True positives (TP) are real overheating notes found; false positives (FP) are other notes incorrectly included; false negatives (FN) are real ones missed. Precision=TP/(TP+FP) asks how trustworthy the returned set is. Recall=TP/(TP+FN) asks how much of the required set was found.

TP=400, FP=50, FN=100. Does the cheap cascade meet recall≥0.9?

Precision=400/450≈0.889; recall=400/500=0.8, so it fails. Lower cost does not fix missing required positives. Choose routing thresholds on a calibration set, then test on separate labeled data. Use public/synthetic data or approved local inference; do not assume permission to transmit private documents to an external provider.

sections.title: Recent systems and what their guarantees mean
sections.html:
The example shows why cost optimization needs a quality definition. LOTUS offers semantic operators parameterized by natural language, with optimized implementations and statistical accuracy guarantees relative to a specified high-quality reference algorithm. Reference agreement and factual truth are different: two models can agree on the same wrong label. Guarantees for individual operators also need care when composed into a pipeline.

DocETL studies document-processing rewrites. Splitting a long document or decomposing a task can expose evidence a single large prompt misses. Its reported evaluation covers four tasks; a rewrite that helps them need not help every document collection.

Predict a failure before implementing: summarizing each chunk may remove a rare exception; deduplication may merge two distinct events; limiting join candidates may remove the only true match. Model choice, prompts, chunking, batching, selective calls and reuse therefore alter both cost and potentially meaning. Read the reference algorithm, label policy, evaluation splits and optimization cost beside any speedup.

Sources for this section: LOTUS (PVLDB 2025); DocETL (PVLDB 2025). Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: A complete quality and cost evaluation
sections.html:
Make the labels concrete before collecting a score. For example: include “battery became too hot to touch”; exclude “battery did not overheat”; mark an unreadable or conflicting note uncertain and retain its evidence span. Have independent annotators resolve disagreements on a sample rather than silently deciding from model output.

Compare deterministic rules where meaningful, one fixed-model pipeline and the optimized pipeline on the same task. Split by source document or entity so near-duplicates cannot leak between development, calibration and test. Choose prompts and thresholds before reading final test labels.

Keep raw output and model/prompt revisions. Report precision, recall, F1 or field errors, important subgroups and unsupported claims. Separately count calls, input/output tokens, assumed price, optimizer search, retries, wall time, p95 and peak memory. A fixed seed need not make every backend identical; repeat when variability affects the decision.

The optimized pipeline agrees with its reference LLM on 98% of notes. Is factual accuracy 98%?

No. That is reference agreement. A separate factual or human-labeled check is needed because the reference can share the optimized model's mistakes. Preserve the 98% agreement result under its correct name.

sections.title: H100-sized mini-experiment: semantic-filter batching and cascades
sections.html:
Trace four held-out notes with independent labels positive, negative, positive, negative. Cheap outputs are positive, negative, uncertain, negative. Only note three goes to the expensive model. If it says positive, final labels recover both positives with one expensive call. If cheap output three had confidently said negative, the expensive stage would never see the missed positive. This is why confidence routing needs recall calibration.

Optional local work can compare batch sizes and context limits with a small licensed open-weight model on public/synthetic documents. Eight billion parameters at two bytes each already require about 16 GB just for weights. The attention key/value cache, activations, workspace and allocator add memory, depending on context length, batch, architecture and implementation. Inspect actual H100 capacity and pinned serving-engine requirements.

Hold prompts, model and quality evaluation fixed while comparing single-model inference with the cascade; load sequentially if needed. Measure complete cost and quality. Two-device replicas and tensor/model parallelism solve different problems and add orchestration or communication; two H100s are not automatically one memory pool. This exercise does not train a foundation model or promise a novel result.

Sources for this section: vLLM Optimization and Tuning. Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: From a prototype to a safe research claim
sections.html:
A useful conclusion names the corpus, label policy, model version, quality target, measured cost and exceptions. “Cheaper” without those conditions leaves the reader unable to decide whether the same task was solved.

You chose a prompt after inspecting every test error, then scored that same set again. How can the study be repaired?

That set has become development data. Freeze the prompt and test on a new held-out set, or report the result as exploratory rather than an unbiased final score. Keep the search budget and alternatives tried. The extra search cost belongs in the experiment even if only the final pipeline is deployed.

Before recommending a shortcut, explain which work it omits and which answers it might change. That causal statement connects query optimization to semantic processing without assuming exact relational equivalence.

Key takeaway

Optimize quality, cost and latency jointly. Every shortcut needs an explicit statement of what it may change.

quiz.question: LOTUS-style agreement with a reference algorithm most directly measures what?
options: Statistical fidelity to the chosen reference behavior.
quiz.explanation: The reference algorithm defines the target for agreement. If both reference and optimized model make the same factual mistake, they still agree. Human/factual truth and effects of composing several operators therefore require separate checks.
quiz.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A deterministic date filter retains 4,000 of 20,000 notes. At $0.002 per LLM call, what is the classification cost after filtering, ignoring other costs?
questions.explanation: After filtering, 4,000 notes each incur $0.002, giving $8. Classifying all 20,000 would cost $40 under the same assumption. The saving is valid only if the date filter preserves the intended question; labeling, optimization, retries and other charges remain separate.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is a sound way to select a semantic-cascade threshold?
options: Choose the threshold that sends no requests to the expensive model.
Use a calibration set, then assess quality and cost on independent test data.
Tune on all final test labels and report that score.
questions.explanation: Routing thresholds are chosen using evidence, so tune them on a calibration set and measure on an independent test set. A confident cheap-model false negative is never sent to the expensive stage. Check recall as well as call cost; confidence alone does not certify quality.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A classifier has 400 true positives, 100 false negatives and 50 false positives. What is recall?
questions.explanation: Actual positives are the 400 found plus the 100 missed: 500. Recall=400/500=0.8. The 50 false positives instead enter precision, 400/(400+50)≈0.889. These answer different questions about missed and incorrect results.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Which text-to-SQL check goes beyond successful execution?
options: Confirm that the query expresses the user’s intended joins, filters and aggregation semantics.
Remove authorization checks for easier testing.
Check only whether SQL has a semicolon.
Assume every returned number is correct.
questions.explanation: A DBMS can execute valid SQL that expresses the wrong question. Inspect schema and intended meaning, joins/duplicates, date boundaries and grouping; also validate permissions and resource use. Successful execution verifies none of those semantic choices by itself.
